title: Ultrasonic Testing for Automotive Plants | UT (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US automotive plants and suppliers: press frames, die blocks, forgings, castings, fixtures. Request a UT inspection quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Automotive Manufacturing Plants in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT provides on-site ultrasonic testing for automotive assembly plants and their suppliers in the United States: press frames and die blocks, forgings and castings, weld fixtures, robot-cell bases and plant utility vessels. Technicians are mobilized to the plant during shutdown weeks or scheduled downtime, examine to the drawing, specification and customer requirement, and report thickness readings and indications for the plant's engineers to act on. For a scope, request a UT inspection quote.

Where ultrasonic testing fits in an automotive plant

An automotive plant is a machine for repeating the same operation millions of times, and the equipment that makes it possible is large, heavily loaded and expected to run for decades. Ultrasonic testing looks inside that equipment. A crack that starts in a press crown or a die block grows with each stroke, and the first outward sign may be a part-quality problem or an unplanned stop. Examining by sound before that point is the reason the method is used on tooling, structures and the forgings and castings that go into vehicles.

The work divides between the assembly plant itself and the supplier base around it: stamping plants, forge shops, foundries, machining plants and weldment suppliers. Our ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings page covers the product-level method; this page covers what is specific to automotive.

The assets we examine

  • Press and die tooling: large forged and cast die blocks, die inserts and sub-plates, where a buried discontinuity in thick tool steel or cast iron can lead to a fracture under load.
  • Press structures: crowns, uprights, bolsters, slides and tie rods on mechanical and hydraulic presses, examined at welds and high-stress locations and by straight-beam scans for thickness and bolt condition.
  • Forgings: crankshaft and axle blanks, gear and ring forgings, connecting rod and steering knuckle blanks at the forge or at receiving inspection.
  • Castings: ductile iron and steel components such as housings, brackets and tooling castings, scanned for internal shrinkage and cracks where the purchase specification calls for it.
  • Weld fixtures and robot cells: base plates, frames and support structures of body-in-white lines, where fatigue cracks develop at weld toes and at bolted joints.
  • Plant utilities: compressed air receivers, process water and hydraulic accumulators, and utility piping, where thickness measurement tracks corrosion; our piping circuit inspection page describes how those thickness locations are organized.

Whose requirements govern

An automotive plant works under its own quality management system, typically built to IATF 16949 with additional customer-specific requirements from each vehicle maker. That system is the plant's, not ours. It sets how nonconforming product is contained, how records are retained and how a supplier's test results are reviewed. We examine to the plant's procedure, or to a written procedure we prepare that the plant adopts, and we report in a form that fits the plant's control plan.

The technical documents depend on the asset. Steel forgings are commonly examined to ASTM A388 and cast components to ASTM A609; weldments follow AWS D1.1 or the customer's weld specification; thickness measurement on plant pressure equipment follows the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII, with the examination technique drawn from ASME Section V. The ultrasonic method for plate and thickness is described in our ultrasonic testing guide and the ASME Section V Article 5 explanation. Plant and customer engineers decide acceptance; we report against the criterion supplied.

Technique details for tooling, forgings and castings

Thick sections of tool steel and cast iron behave differently from the plate of a fabricated weldment. Cast iron and coarse-grained castings scatter and absorb sound, so a lower test frequency is usually needed than for forged steel, and the sensitivity setting differs. Large forgings are scanned with straight beam from several faces against a reference such as a flat-bottom hole or a back-wall echo, with the loss of back-wall echo treated as a signal that something is interrupting the sound path.

  • Reference blocks: the block must match the acoustic properties of the part being examined. A block of the wrong grade or heat treatment gives wrong sensitivity.
  • Surface condition: machined surfaces need little more than couplant; rough as-cast and flame-cut surfaces usually need grinding or a heavier couplant, and the report records what was done.
  • Scanning plan: coverage is defined by drawing or procedure, including the faces scanned, overlap, scan speed and the number of angles used for welds.
  • Geometry: keyways, bores, radii and fillets create false echoes. The technician maps geometry before scanning so a real indication is not confused with a feature of the part.
  • Thickness grids: on press structures and utility vessels, readings are taken at marked grid points so repeat visits compare the same locations.

What UT finds and what it does not

UT detects internal discontinuities in forgings and castings, laminar flaws in plate, cracks that run across the sound beam in welds and a loss of wall thickness from corrosion or wear. It does not find a fine surface crack on a part with a rough surface as reliably as a surface method does, and it does not report the metallurgical properties of the material. Surface-breaking cracks on machined tooling are a job for magnetic particle inspection in automotive plants on steel, and for penetrant testing in automotive plants on aluminum and other non-magnetic parts. Which method suits a given part is part of every scope review we do.

What the UT report contains

Typical contents of an automotive UT report
ItemWhat we record
AssetPlant, line or press number, part number or tag, material and heat or lot where known
ProcedureProcedure and revision, specification, edition and the acceptance criterion supplied by the plant
EquipmentFlaw detector and transducers, frequency, reference block and calibration check results
PersonnelTechnician and level under the written practice, with the Level III reviewing the report
ResultsIndications with location, depth, size and amplitude; thickness grids; accept or reject against the supplied criterion
TraceabilitySketches or marked photographs, so findings link back to a specific location for the plant's records

Press structures, tie rods and fatigue

Presses fail by fatigue more than by overload. Every stroke puts the crown, uprights and tie rods through a load cycle, and a small crack at a weld toe or a thread root grows a little each time. Tie rods and large bolts are a particular case: an ultrasonic examination along the bolt axis can reveal a crack at the first engaged thread, where stress concentrates, without removing the rod. Weld toes on welded press frames are scanned with angle beam from the plate surface, and the technician marks where each scan was made so a follow-up visit repeats the same coverage.

Records matter here as much as findings. A crack that was present and stable at the last shutdown but longer at this one is information an engineer can use; a report that does not tie an indication to a marked location cannot support that comparison. We therefore mark the surface of the structure where practical, photograph the marking, and keep the sketch with the report, so the next examination can be compared with this one rather than starting from zero.

What to send for a quote

  • List of assets or parts, with drawings, material and thickness
  • Specification and acceptance criteria, plus any customer-specific requirement that applies
  • Quantity and examination plan: sample size for receiving inspection or the full list for shutdown work
  • Surface condition and whether grinding or cleaning is the plant's job
  • Access: pits, platforms, lock-out and tag-out requirements and the safe working height
  • Shutdown dates or windows, plant orientation and badging, and the site address

Planning around plant shutdown weeks

Automotive plants run on a build schedule with little slack, and most inspection that needs equipment off happens during planned shutdowns, such as the summer retooling period and the year-end break. Presses, robots and conveyors are locked out and tagged out in sequence, and every trade shares the same limited window. A UT crew arriving without a confirmed lock-out plan loses time that the window cannot give back, so we ask for the lock-out sequence, safe access and the contact who signs the permits before mobilizing.

Where work cannot wait for a shutdown, some thickness measurement and weld examination can be done on idle equipment between shifts. We agree the scope with the plant's maintenance and quality leaders so the findings arrive while the plant can still act on them. Written procedures and qualification demonstrations are available through NDT technical procedure development if the plant needs a documented method.

Where we work in the United States for automotive

These city pages cover the main automotive manufacturing regions where we are asked to mobilize for UT:

  • Detroit: assembly, stamping and tooling suppliers across southeast Michigan.
  • Toledo: powertrain, axle and stamping operations in northwest Ohio.
  • Grand Rapids: tooling, fixture and component suppliers in west Michigan.
  • Fort Wayne: heavy-truck and drivetrain-related manufacturing in northeast Indiana.
  • Columbus: assembly-adjacent suppliers and forge and machining shops across central Ohio.
  • Louisville: assembly and parts suppliers along the Ohio River.
  • Greenville: Upstate South Carolina vehicle and supplier plants.
  • Nashville: Middle Tennessee assembly and component plants.
  • Birmingham: Alabama assembly and supplier operations.
  • Indianapolis: transmission, casting and forge operations across central Indiana.

Training your plant technicians

Plants that keep UT in-house build their own program: UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training give technicians the foundation, and the ultrasonic testing simulator offers calibration and scanning practice without taking presses or parts out of service. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer issues the qualification. For the wider sector see NDT training for manufacturing.

Boundaries of this service

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and specialist ultrasonic techniques are not covered on this page. We do not take over the plant's quality system, we do not decide whether a part is released to a customer, and we do not repair or machine. We provide examination results that the plant's engineers use to accept, scrap, rework or monitor. See also the national ultrasonic testing page.

faq.q: Do you work under our IATF 16949 system?
faq.a: The quality system is the plant's, so we work to your procedures, control plan and customer-specific requirements, or to a written procedure you adopt. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification for its own operations; it does not claim IATF 16949.

faq.q: Can you inspect press frames and die blocks while the press is running?
faq.a: Not safely. Examination of crowns, uprights and die blocks needs the press locked out and tagged out, and access to the surfaces. Some thickness readings on idle equipment can happen between shifts, but most work belongs in a shutdown window.

faq.q: What do you need to quote UT for an automotive plant?
faq.a: Send the asset list with drawings, material and thickness, the specification and acceptance criteria, quantities, surface condition, access and lock-out requirements, shutdown dates and the site address with orientation and badging details.

faq.q: Can UT find cracks in a cast iron die?
faq.a: It can find internal discontinuities and some cracks, but coarse structure in cast iron attenuates sound and limits what can be resolved. For surface cracks on a machined die, magnetic particle inspection is usually the more practical method, and we advise on the mix.

faq.q: Do you examine incoming forgings at the supplier or at our plant?
faq.a: Both. Technicians travel to the forge shop or to your receiving area, scan the forgings against the purchase specification and report each lot. We confirm the sample size and acceptance criteria with you before the crew travels to the site.

faq.q: Who decides whether a part is released?
faq.a: The plant's quality organization decides, using the acceptance criterion in the specification or customer requirement. Our report lists each indication or thickness reading with its location so the decision can be made, but we do not release or reject product.

faq.q: Can you measure wall thickness on compressed air receivers?
faq.a: Yes. Thickness readings on air receivers and utility vessels are taken on a marked grid and compared against the minimum wall set by the plant's engineer or authorized inspector. We provide the readings; the remaining-life judgment belongs to them.

faq.q: Is UT or MT better for fatigue cracks in weld fixtures?
faq.a: Fatigue cracks usually start at weld toes at the surface, so magnetic particle inspection is quicker on steel fixtures. UT adds value when the crack may extend into the weld or the base plate. We often scope both for a critical fixture.

faq.q: Do your technicians hold their own qualifications?
faq.a: They are qualified by Atlantis under its written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II technicians performing and interpreting and an ASNT NDT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. Qualification records can be provided to the plant.
